asDecan.p: Every sign gets cut into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and each slice has its own planet and its own card. Your Sun sits between 10 and 19 degrees of Aries, the middle slice, where the sign has settled in and is at full strength, and in the old Chaldean order that slice belongs to the Sun. The Sun is also exalted in Aries. That's the old word for an honoured guest, a planet shown at its most idealised. Mars still rules the sign, so the drive underneath is Aries all the way through. What the Sun adds is pride in the things you start. You want them to go somewhere, and you want it known whose they were. The slice before yours, the Two of Wands, is Mars in its own sign, pure push. The one after, the Four, is Venus, and it wants company and a party. The Emperor is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside him.

You start things and then you care what becomes of them, which sounds obvious until you've watched a first-decan Aries walk off a project the day it got boring. You send the proposal on Monday and by Wednesday you're checking your inbox every twenty minutes. You organise the group holiday, book the house, send round the spreadsheet, and then take it oddly personally when someone's lukewarm about the restaurant you picked. At the end-of-year work drinks you're the one talking about next year's plan while everyone else is complaining about this one. Have a look at the figure in the picture, up on a cliff with their back to you, watching ships that have already gone out. That's the part you find hardest. The idea's launched, the application's in, there's nothing left to do but let it come back, and honestly you'd take an argument over that sort of waiting.

You're very good at backing other people, and it tends to get missed under all the confidence. The exalted Sun wants things to go well in general, and once it's decided an idea is good it doesn't much mind whose idea it was. A friend mentions over dinner that they'd like to start a small business, and by dessert you've got a name for it, three people for them to ring and a date to have it done by. You write the reference, lend the car, turn up to the first gig and bring six people with you. That's the Sun's part in you. Mars left to itself mostly backs Mars. People remember that sort of help for years, long after you've forgotten giving it. The odd thing is how much slower you are to back your own second attempt, once the first one has gone quiet.

Exaltation is flattering, and it has a catch. A planet in exaltation shows the idealised version of itself, and with the Sun that means the plan in your head is always bigger and quicker than the one that turns up. So you can be let down by something that's going fine. The kitchen renovation is on budget and two weeks late, and you talk about it like a disaster. The little podcast has forty regular listeners after three months, which is good, and you decide nobody cares. The other habit is checking on things so often you get in their way. You ring the agent for news, you rewrite the pitch after one silence, you ask the builder for a new finish date every Friday. I've known people with this decan pull a perfectly good application after two quiet weeks and send in a worse one.

When something goes wrong, the Aries part moves first. You get busy, you make five calls, you've got a new plan inside the hour, and anyone who suggests sleeping on it gets short shrift. If the blow lands on something you'd put your name to, the job that didn't come through, the business that folded, the engagement you'd announced, the Sun part takes it personally, and about a week later that shows. You go flat and slightly grand about it, saying things like 'it was never going to work anyway'. The people around you get whiplash, first from the energy and then from the sulk, and your partner can end up doing the grieving for both of you. What helps is physical and dull. Proper sleep, daylight, a long walk, and one person who asks what you'd actually hoped would happen and lets you answer without fixing it.

Third date and you've half planned the trip to Japan, and you mean it, which is lovely and also a lot for someone who was still deciding whether they liked you. Part of what you fall for is the future you've pictured with them, and a partner can usually tell when they've been cast in it. Once you've chosen someone you talk them up to everyone, and you want them to do well out in the world. Where it goes wrong is timing. A slow reply to a text, a partner who needs a weekend to think about moving in, and you read it as a no when it's usually someone going at their own speed. You also like to be the one with the ideas. Let them start something now and then, the holiday, the Friday night habit, the new friends, and go along with it without improving it.

At work you want to run something, and you want it to reach past the building you're sitting in. Interstate clients, an export order, a cold pitch to someone who's never heard of you, that kind of distance suits this slice of Aries well. You're good in the first year of anything, better than most at getting a team to commit, and fine with being the one who has to answer for it. The part that needs a system is the long gap between sending something out and hearing back. Grant rounds, sales cycles, a manuscript sitting with an agent. Keep two or three things moving at once so no single silence gets all your attention. You also do better work on something people know is yours, so arrange for that where you can, even if it's only the byline on a report.

At twenty this decan usually looks like a lot of launches and not much follow-through, partly because nothing comes back fast enough to hold your interest. You're sure of yourself in a way older people find either charming or exhausting. By the mid-thirties the pattern tends to shift, because some of what you sent out in your twenties finally comes back. A qualification pays off, a contact from years ago rings with a job, and you learn that waiting is sometimes the actual work. Most people with a Sun here get noticeably better at patience in that decade, though it never becomes their favourite thing. The fifties often bring a taste for backing younger people's ventures, investing, mentoring, lending your name. The risk then is judging every new plan by how your own went, and forgetting how long yours took to come good.

Next time you send out something that matters, the application, the pitch, the message you rewrote four times, work out the date you'd reasonably expect an answer and put it in your calendar. Then leave it alone until that day. No chasing, no checking the sent folder, no redrafting it in your head at two in the morning. When the itch comes, go and start something small and unrelated, fix the gate, cook something you've never made. On the day, follow up once, politely.
